The core concept of primary reinforcement emerges from experimental observation of behavioral selection under aversive stimuli. In this context, the rat's behavior evolves through trial-and-error until it selects the most effective escape mechanism—leaping the barrier—before the shock activates. This reflects a fundamental principle of learning where certain actions become more probable due to their association with positive outcomes or reduced negative consequences. The mathematical formulation treats reinforcement as a probabilistic update of action-value functions, where the likelihood of selecting R4 increases with repeated success. Selective learning arises from competition among several possible responses (R1, Rg, Rs, R4), each initiated by the same initial drive D but differing in outcome predictability. Differential strengthening implies that neural pathways associated with successful outcomes gain synaptic weight, while those linked to failure lose efficacy. These processes can be modeled using Markov decision processes or reinforcement learning kernels, where the reward signal modulates transition probabilities between states defined by sensory inputs and motor outputs.
